title: Crafts
description: Bidriware, Paithani silk, Hyderabadi pearls and Deccan miniatures — the material culture of the Deccan.
dedication: In memory of the Asaf Jahi dynasty
subtitle: Bidriware, Paithan silk, Hyderabadi pearls, Deccan miniatures

items.value: Bidriware registered as a Geographical Indication (GI) of India

sections.sub: The signature craft of Bidar, made nowhere else on earth
body: Bidriware — the signature craft of Bidar — has been made the same way for more than five centuries. A vessel of zinc-and-copper alloy is cast, scored with a steel point, inlaid with hammered silver and brass wire, and then dipped in a paste of soil from the Bidar fort that turns the alloy a deep matte black.<cite data-ref="michell-zebrowski-1999"></cite> The silver, untouched, gleams against it. No other metalwork looks like it; it is registered as a Geographical Indication (GI) of India.

items.value: Bidar, since c. 1500 — silver-inlaid blackened alloy.
Paithan, since c. 200 BCE — pure-silk sari with zari tapestry borders.
Hyderabad — drilling and stringing techniques perfected under the Nizams.
Aurangabad — silk-and-cotton brocade, a courtly textile of the Mughal Deccan.
Hand-painted cotton with vegetable dyes; flourished under the Golconda court.
Hyderabadi Choodi Bazaar tradition — stone-set lacquer bangles in every shade.

sections.sub: The tapestry-bordered sari of the looms south of Aurangabad
body: South of Aurangabad, the looms of Paithan have woven the Paithani sari since the Satavahana age — pure mulberry silk with a tapestry-woven border in real zari, taking up to a year for one piece. Hyderabad's pearl trade, fed by the Persian Gulf and the Coromandel coast, made the city the world's pearl capital under the Nizams; the bazaar at Charminar still sells more pearls than any place on earth.

sections.sub: The Deccan school of miniature — taller and more lyrical than the Mughal
body: The painted arts had their own school. The Deccan miniature, born at Ahmadnagar and refined at Bijapur and Golconda, used taller proportions, lyrical landscapes and a palette of emerald, lapis and gold leaf — closer to Persian Safavid taste than to the Mughal manner of Delhi.<cite data-ref="zebrowski-1983"></cite>

items.text: The Paithani sari tradition is established at Paithan in the Satavahana age — pure mulberry silk with tapestry-woven zari borders, each piece taking up to a year to complete.

With the Bahmani Sultanate, Persian metalworking techniques arrive at Bidar and the Deccan develops its distinctive court material culture across metal, textile, and painted arts.<cite data-ref="michell-zebrowski-1999"></cite>

Bidriware is codified at Bidar: zinc-and-copper vessels inlaid with hammered silver wire and blackened using soil unique to the Bidar fort — a technique that survives nowhere else on earth.<cite data-ref="michell-zebrowski-1999"></cite>

The Deccan miniature school is born at Ahmadnagar and spreads to Bijapur and Golconda, developing taller proportions, lyrical landscapes, and a palette of emerald, lapis, and gold leaf closer to Safavid Persia than to Mughal Delhi.<cite data-ref="zebrowski-1983"></cite>

Kalamkari — hand-painted cotton using vegetable dyes — flourishes under the Golconda court; Himroo silk-and-cotton brocade is established at Aurangabad as a courtly textile of the Mughal Deccan.<cite data-ref="michell-zebrowski-1999"></cite>

Hyderabad's pearl trade — fed by the Persian Gulf and the Coromandel coast — reaches its zenith under the Asaf Jahi Nizams; the city becomes the world's leading pearl market.<cite data-ref="leonard-1978"></cite>

The bazaar near Charminar still sells more pearls than any place on earth; Bidriware is registered as a Geographical Indication (GI) of India; and the Paithani and Himroo looms continue in Paithan and Aurangabad.

references.text: George Michell & Mark Zebrowski, Architecture and Art of the Deccan Sultanates (The New Cambridge History of India I.7), Cambridge University Press, 1999.
Mark Zebrowski, Deccani Painting, University of California Press, 1983.
Karen Leonard, Social History of an Indian Caste: The Kayasths of Hyderabad, University of California Press, 1978.
